newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Serbia law would lift restrictions on the press.
newsitem.headline: Serbia law would lift restrictions on the press.

text.p: The Serbian government, under pressure to free the state-dominated media, unveiled an amended version of a new press law on Friday that would lift restrictions on privately-owned newspapers and broadcasters.
The new draft, which could become law in May but is still liable to change, guarantees freedom from censorship.
"I am convinced that the new version will create an atmosphere conducive to futher democratisation in the country," Serbian Information Minister Radmila Milentijevic told a news conference.
Serbia's media is dominated by state radio and television and the daily Politika, both tightly controlled by Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic's Socialist party (SPS).
The West, which has maintained an outer wall of sanctions against Belgrade barring it from foreign funding, has pressed Milosevic to ensure press freedoms.

The Zajedno (Together) coalition of opposition parties, which is seeking to break a socialist stranglehold on the press, has threatened to boycott presidential and parliamentary elections without concessions on press freedom.
The government's earlier version of the proposed press law fell well short of the demands of Zajedno, which has won a long battle to take control of Belgrade and other towns from the socialists.
Anti-monopoly clauses in the previous draft said no private radio or television station would be allowed to broadcast to an audience of more than 25 percent of the 10.5 million population.
No individual or organisation could have held more than 20 percent of the newspapers and magazines published in Serbia.
Also dropped is a provision requiring publications and broadcasters to declare foreign funding or assistance.

In another positive trend, the socialist-controlled Serbian Television network dropped attempts last month to stop Serbia's most trusted and watched independent BK Television from broadcasting across the country.
